item.title: Republican billionaire Rick Jackson walks a Trump tightrope in Georgia governor bid
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
ATLANTA (AP) — He's hardly the first billionaire to promise working-class voters he'll fight for them in public office. Rick Jackson , the Republican candidate for Georgia governor, has even compared himself to the real estate mogul who reached the Oval Office. But Jackson’s path differs from Donald Trump’s , and the 72-year-old healthcare magnate and investor brings a vastly different persona to his first campaign. Unlike Trump, who was born to wealth , Jackson spent his early years bouncing through foster homes before launching his first company as a young man. Now, he wants to leverage both his similarities and contrasts with the president, a challenge he's tackling with buckets of his own campaign cash and a personal story that anchors his appeal to voters. “I have lived in poverty,” Jackson says. “When you have not eaten, you never forget that, and you don’t forget the people that are struggling.” Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms , a former Atlanta mayor, disputes Jackson’s altruistic pitch, setting up the Nov. 3 election as a test of whether an alternate, softer version of conservative billionaire politics can complement or even counter Trump’s pugilistic populism in a key swing state. Jackson planned to join Trump at a rally Saturday in Perry, in what would be his second appearance with the president in the closing stretch of the campaign. ‘From foster care to billionaire’ “My father left me at nine months old. My mother was a sixth-grade educated waitress with a severe alcohol problem,” Jackson said in the only debate of their general election campaign. “I had seven stepfathers before I was 12. I lived in the projects, went to 13 different schools, and lived in five different foster homes.” He left college to start a business at 21. That led to Jackson Healthcare, a behemoth company that provides contract nurses and other workers to hospitals and health systems, including public entities that have helped fuel Jackson’s fortunes with taxpayer money. At events with supporters, Jackson gets more personal. “I have, because of my background, severe abandonment issues,” he told hundreds of voters in Cleveland, a conservative enclave in the north Georgia mountains. He turns that acknowledgment into a promise: “Let me tell you one thing: I will never abandon you.” Rags-to-riches themes are not uncommon in politics, and it’s yielded Jackson’s campaign motto: “From foster care to billionaire.” But the scale is eye-popping, illuminated by the nearly $200 million Jackson has spent personally on the campaign. That puts him among the largest self-funding candidates in the history of American elections. But on that score, too, Jackson tries to soften the caricature of the billionaire executive. “It’s not my money,” he said in a northern suburb of Atlanta. Jackson calls his fortune “God’s money” and says that “my job is to have kingdom impact” with it. “The reason I have spent so much money to do this,” he said, is to “help 11 million Georgians, to keep them from struggling.” A range of images over a long campaign Jackson launched his bid as a relative unknown, though Capitol insiders knew him because of Jackson Healthcare, its lucrative state contracts and his lobbying interest in healthcare, business and tax policy. The Republican primary field featured a trio of statewide elected officials, including Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, who won Trump’s endorsement in August 2025 , before Jackson got in. During the primary, Jackson embraced the president even though he wasn't Trump's choice. Jackson sometimes promised to “be like Trump, but with Southern tone.” He pledged to “deliver for Georgia the same type of business solutions that President Trump is bringing to our country.” Largely aligning himself with Trump on immigration, Jackson promised to make Georgia a national leader in deportations. “I don’t care if you’re Muslim or Mongolian, you don’t have the right to force your culture on our country,” he said in one ad. “Criminal illegals” who “commit sick, violent crimes” would “end up deported or departed,” he promised. Soon after defeating Jones in a runoff, Jackson shelved the immigration ad, but not before using it as part of a spot featuring his grandchildren. “Granddad, why do you look so mean in these ads?” one asks after watching the “deported or departed” clip on her phone. The children and teenagers then tell their grandfather how he can “look cool” with a pickup truck, a dog and a hipper wardrobe. “Let’s make Georgia better together,” the redressed Jackson concludes. He has since circulated an ad with several young adults who benefited from the millions he spent helping foster children who age out of the Georgia system when they turn 18. “I am so proud of you,” he tells them as he chokes up. On policy, Republican fare and centrist appeals As he softens his image, Jackson maintains traditional Republican positions, pledging to cut taxes, regulation and what he describes as waste. If he cannot halve the state income tax in four years, he promises not to seek a second term. He wants a balanced budget and full audits of state spending, without saying state law requires a balanced budget and audits of state agencies have long been standard practice. He says he will expand healthcare without expanding Medicaid under the 2010 Affordable Care Act. Instead, he argues he can fund broader coverage through partnerships with private insurers. That would require Washington to grant permission and commit a level of financial support that no state has gotten without expanding the traditional Medicaid program. Jackson says he can do all of that while increasing spending on teacher salaries and vocational education. At the same time, he has toned down his Trump adulation, reflecting Georgia’s general election math and voters' frustrations with the Iran war and inflation. In July, Jackson stood with Trump in Marietta and expressed his hope to “be this guy’s favorite governor.” When Trump returned to Dalton on Oct. 16, Jackson did not mention Trump at all in his own speech. Later, when the president called him on stage, Jackson praised Trump — for advocating for foster children. When Trump announced that he would be back to Georgia on Saturday, Jackson's campaign initially planned its own event in metro Atlanta before changing it up so Jackson would again be with the president. Bottoms disputes Jackson's everyman appeal Bottoms says Jackson is “trying to buy this election” so he can be a Trump stooge. And Democrats have seized on the way that Jackson has talked about the economy. Discussing trade schools, Jackson said on the debate stage that “my plumber drives a Mercedes.” Discussing inflation and crime during his town hall-style debate with Bottoms, he suggested Atlantans felt unsafe “at the gas store” during her tenure. When a citizen in the debate audience asked Jackson about minimum wage and affording basic necessities, Jackson told her, “Hopefully, you’re not the one that is getting the $7.50 an hour.” Minimum wage is $7.25. Bottoms has proposed doubling it. Jackson has not proposed any increase. “My focus is creating jobs,” he said. “I’ve been creating jobs my entire life.” Jackson's balancing act is enough for Debbie Satterfield, a 72-year-old who came to a Jackson rally in White County wearing both a Trump shirt and a Jackson sticker. “When I heard about his harsh upbringing, and to hear how far he had climbed, and starting from nothing,” she said. “It reminds me of my life starting with nothing. You can see his soul.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/republican-billionaire-rick-jackson-walking-163846161.html

item.title: GOP and Democrats fight for swing voters in a crucial Pennsylvania district
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick speaks during a news conference at the US Capitol in March 2024. - Tierney L. Cross/Bloomberg/Getty Images GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick was weaving through the crowd of a fall street festival when he was confronted by a man enraged by the skyrocketing costs he’s experiencing. Dave Woods, a contractor and registered Democrat, held up red signs with big white letters in Fitzpatrick’s face to show how his heating oil and diesel fuel costs have shot up in the last year. But Fitzpatrick walked away to head to his speech. “Where’s Mr. Fitzpatrick to get in the photo shot here?” Woods told CNN after the exchange. “I’m against the party that caused this.” Farther down the street, Ted Wassmer, a registered Republican who has supported the congressman in the past, was weighing his vote in the November election. Wassmer’s woodworking business has been hit hard by the Trump administration’s tariffs and rising inflation. A combat veteran who has never supported President Donald Trump, Wassmer called the Iran war an “absolute joke.” “It’s a clown show in DC right now,” Wassmer said. “I may vote against Republicans having dominance of the Congress, that may be my decision to get the administration in check. And I’m not very happy with Democrats either. I kind of think the left and the right are running rampant right now, so I have to kind of really look at it.” Fitzpatrick is one of the only Republicans in Congress fighting for reelection in a district Kamala Harris won in 2024 — and Democrats see this as their best chance in a decade to win the seat. unknown content item - Following the congressman on a recent day of campaigning offered an inside look at how the vulnerable Republican is trying to hold onto his battleground district in the suburbs of Philadelphia despite a toxic political environment for his party. Woods was not the only frustrated voter to come up to the congressman with complaints. But Fitzpatrick believes he can keep his seat by distancing himself from his own party and attempting to find common ground. “If they’re angry at Pete Hegseth, take it out on Pete Hegseth. If they’re angry at Donald Trump or Joe Biden or Kamala Harris, take it out on them at the ballot box, but don’t take it out on people that are not them that have never espoused their views,” Fitzpatrick told CNN in a wide-ranging interview. Describing himself as politically homeless in the two-party system, Fitzpatrick says he would register as an independent if Pennsylvania opens its primaries to independent voters and lowers the threshold for independent candidates to get on the ballot. “I’m a registered Republican from when I was 18, but I did that because of Ronald Reagan. That party no longer exists,” Fitzpatrick said. But Democrats plan to use his party affiliation against him . Nationally, Democrats have become increasingly confident they will win the House, hoping that voter concerns over the status quo will lead to losses for Republicans. A new CNN poll found Trump’s approval rating stands at a record low, and voters express broad dissatisfaction with the economy and the state of the country nearly two years into unified GOP control of the federal government. Fitzpatrick’s Democratic challenger, Bucks County Commissioner Bob Harvie, hopes to tap into voter frustration and reluctance to support the Republican ticket to flip the district and bring his party one step closer to reclaiming the House majority. Bob Harvie greets people during an "Autumn Alive" community celebration in Quakertown, Pennsylvania, last Saturday. - Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images “He’s changed. He’s not the same guy he was when we sent him there. You know, he’s a guy that was supposed to fight against corruption as a former FBI agent, and this is the most corrupt administration in American history. And he’s not doing anything about it,” Harvie told CNN. “He hasn’t stood up for the people here, and plus we’ve got the mood of this country and the pain that people are feeling is different than anything that’s happened before.” Fitzpatrick has withstood national headwinds before, including the blue wave of 2018 when Democrats flipped the House. Democrats believe, however, that his attempts to distance himself from his party now might not be enough to overcome the palpable anger of many of his constituents, and are investing millions in this race for the first time in six years as a result. Democrats have spent over $10 million in advertisements since September, according to AdImpact. Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro has also invested heavily in the race and has appeared with Harvie on the campaign trail. Democrats knew going into the final stretch that Bucks County voters have a history of making their decisions late in the game, which is in part why national Democratic groups started ramping up their spending in the district in the final weeks, according to a Democratic strategist working on House races. To defend against the influx of Democratic cash, the Republican fundraising apparatus has parachuted in, including $100,000 from super PAC MAGA Inc., according to Federal Election Commission filings, and $4.9 million from the Republican outside campaign arm earlier this month for advertisements. In a sign of how difficult the race has become, Fitzpatrick spent $5 million of his own war chest between July and September. “They take their shots when the climate is such that they think that, you know, that it’s a wise investment for them,” Fitzpatrick said of Democrats. “So, they think.” The two candidates have not faced off directly to debate, even though both have made offers. Fitzpatrick, a former FBI agent, has claimed Harvie has been the subject of an FBI investigation, while Harvie says he never was and argues Fitzpatrick is trying to recycle old claims. But all of the mudslinging on television and posturing online hasn’t necessarily translated to real life. On Saturday, when the two candidates had a chance encounter as they both waited to speak at an event in Bristol, they ignored each other. Breaking down the race Campaign signage for Rep. Fitzpatrick is displayed in Quakertown last Saturday. - Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images Four swing districts in Pennsylvania could be key to winning control of the House in November. On paper, Fitzpatrick’s seat should be the easiest for Democrats to flip given his left-leaning district, but the congressman’s voting record and endorsement list make it difficult for Democrats to easily put him in a box, and Democrats privately concede this is their hardest race in the state, according to multiple Democratic operatives and sources. Fitzpatrick was one of two House Republicans to vote against Trump’s signature package of tax and federal spending cuts in July, dubbed the “big beautiful bill,” even though he was a decisive vote for an earlier version of the legislation that passed the House in May. He has voted to rein in Trump’s war with Iran, but only after it passed the 60-day clock on the use of military force without congressional authorization. He recently signed on to a new effort to force a vote on releasing more of the Jeffrey Epstein files. He did not back an initial effort to force a vote to compel the Justice Department to release millions of pages of files, but he did vote in favor of that earlier Epstein files push when it came to the floor. And on multiple occasions, he has helped Democrats bring their legislation to the floor. Fitzpatrick has signed on to more discharge petitions — a maneuver to circumvent House GOP leadership to bring bills to the floor — than any other Republican this Congress. He was early to sound the alarm that Republicans did not have a plan to address the affordability crisis, and he worked with Democrats in the House to try to extend the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired at the end of 2025. He is a fierce advocate for Ukraine and vowed to end Trump’s unpopular $1.8 billion compensation fund that critics said would be used to pay out the president’s allies. He’s the only Republican running for federal office to receive an endorsement from the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the country. In 2024, Fitzpatrick voted for former UN Ambassador Nikki Haley for president, snubbing Trump. Former Sen. Joe Manchin, who dropped his Democratic party affiliation to become an independent, told CNN that he endorsed Fitzpatrick because of their strong working relationship in Congress. Rep. Fitzpatrick listens to Sen. Joe Manchin as they attend a news conference in Washington, DC, in March 2022. - Jacquelyn Martin/AP “I don’t look at the party, I look at the person, and I got to be honest with you, Brian is just the right person to be serving. I don’t even know the other gentleman. I’m sure he’s an upstanding person. I never go out and campaign against anybody. I just know when you’ve got a good one, you ought to keep him,” Manchin told CNN. “The Democrats will be able to work with Brian as well as they will anybody else if it’s good for our country.” Harvie has looked to poke holes in Fitzpatrick’s voting record and argued that his votes against his party either are inconsistent or don’t change the outcome. He has questioned why Fitzpatrick is receiving money from the Republican Party if he claims to be an independent voice. And while Fitzpatrick meets with various groups throughout the district, Harvie has questioned why the congressman hasn’t held a formal town hall in years. “I don’t really know the last time he’s cast a vote that matters against the president,” Harvie argued. “The president and (House Majority Leader) Mike Johnson have been putting millions of dollars into his campaign to boost him up because they’re afraid he’s going to lose. So, if he’s really that independent, why doesn’t he give that money back?” ‘I’m upset’: Undecided voters still weighing critical vote Both candidates have their work cut out for them in the final two weeks before Election Day. Even with the onslaught of ads and campaign events, there are still voters in the district who say they haven’t made up their minds. But some of Fitzpatrick’s supporters are having a particularly hard time given their broader frustrations with Trump and the Republican Party. Retired Air Force member Nathaniel Gagum is a registered Republican who has voted for Fitzpatrick in the past but says he has been horrified by some of the administration’s military actions and its treatment of veterans. Gagum, who referred to Trump as a “draft dodger,” is furious that Trump fired Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. C.Q. Brown . He says the Iran war should never have happened, and he could not believe Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth outlined plans for a public livestream of a firing squad execution. (Trump later called off the plan for the livestream after public outcry.) “I’m upset,” Gagum, who said he is still undecided, told CNN. Referring to Fitzpatrick, he said , “I’m questioning a lot because of some of the things I see in Congress and how you vote with Congress, and how you side with Trump, and you side with things that goes against our interests, my interests, my veterans.” Becky Berg, a nurse and a registered Libertarian, has voted for Fitzpatrick in previous elections. But she told CNN her costs have gotten more expensive in the last two years, and she is worried about the rights of her LGBTQ+ friends and family who she says have been targeted by some of the Trump administration’s policies. “Honestly, I’m just thinking about getting Republicans out of office for the most part. I will, before I vote, I will look into the candidates and try and be as informed as I can be. But I am not a fan of Trump and a lot of the policies he has been pushing. So, I’m kind of just looking at changing the current regime,” Berg told CNN. Campaign signs for Harvie are seen in Quakertown last Saturday. - Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images In a potential warning sign for Democrats hoping for staying power beyond a potential wave this cycle, a number of Pennsylvania voters who said they were going to support Harvie said their support was more reactionary to the current environment than about Harvie himself. “I think the biggest thing is it’s less about pro-Bob Harvie and more anti-Fitzpatrick. I just don’t think that he does everything that he’s claimed that he’s wanted to do, and I think it’s time for somebody else to be given a shot,” Julia Corrado, a social media manager, told CNN of her intended vote for Harvie. If Fitzpatrick is able to overcome the environment, it will be because of voters like Joe, a 70-year-old retired EPA worker, who went up to Fitzpatrick on Saturday to shake his hand and share that he can separate his frustration with Trump (whom he called a “slime ball”) from the congressman. “I’m a realist. I look at each individual,” he said. ‘I’m done’: The nonvoters Some Pennsylvanians have felt so let down by their leaders that they have given up on the electoral process and plan either not to vote or to write in their own candidate. Jason Green, a restaurant owner of 20 years, sat in his empty cheesesteak shop in Langhorne during what should have been the middle of a weekend dinnertime rush. “It’s at the point where it’s almost not worth being in business,” Green said. Green, a registered independent, voted for Trump in 2024 after initially supporting Robert F. Kennedy Jr. He told CNN he challenged both Fitzpatrick and Harvie to donate the money they were raising for their campaigns to the local community, but said both declined. He plans to write in a different name on the ballot as a result. “I’ve checked out,” Green said. “They’re both idiots in my eyes. Simple as that. I’m done.” About an hour away on the opposite side of the district, John Barchard, 43, was resolved in his decision to not participate in the midterm election. Barchard, who works in marketing, has never been registered with either party and has voted for both Democrats and Republicans. He voted for Harris in 2024; in 2020, he supported former Joe Biden; and he’s supported Fitzpatrick in the past. But now, his frustration with both parties has reached a boiling point because he says neither has done enough to address the needs of the working class. He views Republicans as having capitulated to Trump and criticizes Democrats for not fighting hard enough. John Barchard, 43, in Quakertown, Pennsylvania. - Annie Grayer/CNN “It’s not a ‘what’s the point?’ It’s, ‘I don’t want blood on my hands anymore’ because every time we vote one way, it doesn’t balance out the other, in my opinion. And there needs to be more options,” Barchard told CNN. “The system is not working for anybody.” But somehow, Barchard says he still has hope. “For some dumb reason, as a millennial, I still love this country and I still think it works. I think the experiment is great and it’s taken a wrong turn,” he said. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/24/politics/pennsylvania-swing-seat-midterms

item.title: Police fire tear gas and arrest dozens as France sees more protests
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Nearly 1,000 people were arrested in nationwide protests in France, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said Saturday, after demonstrations over the high cost of living and the country's education system earlier in the day remained largely peaceful. Nuñez said the number of arrests is expected to rise. He said marches "passed off well" in cities, but police officers found themselves confronted with "an extremely elevated level of violence" from "ultra-left" groups later in the day. Nuñez said some shops and businesses had been looted, but "the scale was far smaller" than a week earlier, when some 3,000 businesses were damaged or looted. He said police acted more rapidly and conducted more pre-demonstration checks. Businesses and shopping centers had also been better protected. Earlier Saturday, the interior minister said police had confiscated weapons including metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, he said. The French Interior Ministry said about 410,000 people participated in protests around the country . Union organizers from the General Confederation of Labor put the number at around 800,000. An explanation for the discrepancy was not immediately available. Some confrontations were reported between authorities and demonstrators in several cities, but as of Saturday evening there had been no repeat of the major street violence and rioting that erupted amid similar protests last week. Nuñez previously said that French authorities were preparing to maintain order this weekend by maintaining up to 70,000 officers nationwide along with assets including helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons. Nuñez said authorities will remain "on high alert" overnight and into Saturday. Clashes break out in Paris after largely peaceful march Paris had prepared for unrest, with shops boarded up and events including those related to the NFL's first French football game canceled, but authorities described the atmosphere in the city as "calm." Thousands gathered at the Porte d'Italie on the city's southeastern rim for an authorized demonstration. The march had originally been set for the Bastille, near the city's center, and was changed to the more remote Porte d'Italie at the last minute. Union representative Murielle Guilbert told reporters that it was "scandalous" that Macron had forbidden protesters from demonstrating "where we wish to demonstrate," but participants complied with the change. The front of the march ended without incident. Some chanted "We are not happy" as they peeled away from the Porte de Vincennes. Police said 110,000 people participated in the event, while union members put the number at 250,000. As the evening went on, clashes were reported between police and demonstrators, the Agence France-Presse reported. Nuñez said that "several thousand radical activists" had "gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters." Clashes between protesters and police lasted about two hours, he said. The Paris prosecutor's office said 64 people, including six minors, were arrested and 40 were placed in police custody. Most arrests concerned suspected weapons offenses or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage, the office said. More than 3,000 were stopped and checked by officers, police said. Protesters march against far-right gathering In Orleans, thousands of people marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party. Le Pen is launching her campaign to succeed Emmanuel Macron as France's president. Elections will be held in six months, and surveys show Le Pen is best-placed to win. Demonstrators in Orleans protested both Macron and Le Pen. "Macron resign. Le Pen in prison," the crowd yelled, according to the AFP. Police put their numbers at 11,000, while organizers said 26,000 took part. About 50 organizations, including labor unions, left-wing parties and student groups, had called for a protest against Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration party. Some placards seen at the march referenced a shooting in Trappes , a Paris suburb, that left one person dead and several others injured across several locations. Macron called the rampage a "racist terror attack." Prosecutors are investigating the shooting as a terrorist incident. French media reported that the protest against the congress ended peacefully early Saturday afternoon. The gathering is expected to continue through Sunday. Protesters and police clash in smaller cities Demonstrations had been banned in the southeast city of Lyon, but about 150 protesters near the city's center briefly tried to block a road. Police fired tear gas to disperse the group. Tear gas was also used to break up a group of around 1,000 people gathered in the south of the city. A police helicopter was seen flying over the city, and security forces, armored vehicles and riot police vans were patrolling. A 21-year-old student, who spoke to the Agence France-Presse on the condition of anonymity, described authorities as "really mobile." Water cannons were used in Nice, where demonstrations had also been banned. In the western city of Nantes, thousands of protesters broke through police lines to enter the city center, the AFP reported. Officers used tear gas and a water cannon to try and disperse them. Some on the fringes of the demonstration threw projectiles and aimed fireworks at officers. Police said about 17,000 attended an event in Marseille. Officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march's endpoint. Tear gas was also deployed in Clermont-Ferrand and Strasbourg, police said. Nuñez said one person was seriously injured in Clermont-Ferrand, but did not provide any details. In the city of Toulouse, a 20-year-old man reportedly had fingers blown off, Nuñez said. He did not provide more details about the person, their condition, or how they came to be injured. Nuñez said that in the southern cities of Cannes and Montpellier, authorities saw far-right activists who claimed they were there to protect businesses or sought confrontations with "ultra-left militants." He said it was the first time authorities witnessed this phenomenon. Organizers call for Halloween demonstrations One group of protesters, the Yellow Vests, said they would hold another round of protests on Oct. 31. The Yellow Vests emerged about eight years ago as a loosely organized group that staged disruptive protests against Macron. Organizers called for rallies and a sit-in outside parliament and city halls nationwide, condemning the "authoritarian drift" of Macron's government and urging citizens to stand up for "public freedoms." The demonstrations have been ongoing since September, when high school students in the southeast of Paris protested for better conditions. The unrest quickly spread across the country as people took to the streets to demand relief from rising living costs. More protests spread across Europe Other protests are expected across Europe on Saturday, encompassing a broad range of issues including pensions, housing costs, anti-war movements, education and corruption. Italy deployed soldiers to Milan, the nation's fashion and finance capital, as the city braced for fresh demonstrations one week after looting and police clashes. Many stores were boarded up with wooden planks on Saturday. Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters. In Rome, authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up patrols around key sites. Several hundred students demonstrated peacefully in the historic city. Organizers of peaceful events sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and their hands visible. In Albania's capital of Tirana, riot police used water cannons to subdue large groups of protesters. Some of the demonstrators threw projectiles at police, the AP reported. A separate protest organized by the opposition outside the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama turned violent earlier Saturday, with some activists lighting fires on the street. The demonstrators are mainly high school and university students, demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. A broader anti-government movement is calling for Rama's resignation. In Spain, thousands of retirees and others marched through central Madrid to demand that public pensions aren't meddled with. Protesters in Lisbon, Portugal, are expected to march across the city Saturday to demand affordable housing. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/paris-france-new-protests-riots-museums-shops/

item.title: DOJ wants California to set aside 20,000 voters' ballots. The state is refusing.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Justice Department is pressing California election officials to set aside mail-in ballots from people it believes are noncitizens. It is warning that officials who count those ballots could face criminal charges. Federal prosecutors sent letters Friday to county election offices across the state, giving them 48 hours to work with federal agencies to determine who on a government list is a citizen. NBC News reported that the letters went to 57 of California’s 58 counties. Los Angeles County received a similar letter last week. The secretary of state and Los Angeles County have refused the demand, and other counties are weighing their response. The fight is now before a federal appeals court, 10 days before Election Day. Here’s what to know. What is the Justice Department asking for? The department wants counties to “segregate — not cancel” the mail-in ballots of people on its list until their citizenship can be confirmed, according to a letter to San Bernardino County obtained by NBC News . That county’s list included 1,133 names. It also asked counties to send identifying information about the voters on the list, including Social Security numbers and copies of their registrations, the AP reported . “Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy,” said Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, who signed the letters. Why does the administration say it’s necessary? The Department of Homeland Security compared California’s voter registration files with federal immigration records. It flagged more than 20,000 people it says are “likely” noncitizens who are registered to vote, according to a Justice Department release . Under California law, every registered voter is mailed a ballot. Only U.S. citizens may vote in federal and state elections. “Even one noncitizen vote cancels out the ballot of an American citizen,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in the release. Essayli says the request is limited. “We’re not asking California to take any drastic steps other than to sequester the ballots from the suspected noncitizens,” he told Fox News . Why is California refusing? State officials say the federal data hasn’t been verified, and that acting on it could keep eligible citizens from voting. In court filings, lawyers for the state argued that counties lack both the authority and the federal records needed to check citizenship. They also said the demand could delay certification of the results. Some ballots can’t be pulled back at all. Once a mail-in ballot’s signature is verified, it is separated from its envelope and counted with the others. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed, according to court filings. Dean Logan, the county’s top election official, said the letters carry “a posture of intimidation and threats” just before the election, CNN reported . Sen. Alex Padilla, a Democrat of California, said the administration “has not provided any evidence for their claims of massive voter fraud.” How common is noncitizen voting? Cases do happen, but reviews have found very few. In 2024, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, a Republican, audited the state’s voter rolls and found 20 noncitizens among about 8.2 million registered voters. Federal claims have not always held up. In August, DHS told Nevada officials it had flagged about 15,900 possible noncitizen registrants. It later said that number was preliminary and that it had confirmed only 185 through manual review, CNN reported . In September, Nevada officials said their own review found that all 185 were U.S. citizens. DHS disputes that finding. What does this mean for California voters? For now, nothing has changed. No court has ordered California to set aside any ballots, and counties are still processing the ballots voters return. Voters can check the status of their ballot through the secretary of state’s ballot tracking tool . What happens next? item.title: This U.S. house district was once a political battleground. A new map changed that.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
RALEIGH, N.C. (AP) — In 2022, Democrat Wiley Nickel ran as a moderate and narrowly won North Carolina’s 13th Congressional District by about 9,000 votes. Two years later, the current congressman, Republican Brad Knott, ran as a conservative and coasted into the U.S. House by more than 70,000 votes. Voters didn’t change their minds. Politicians changed their voters. North Carolina’s Republican-controlled legislature redrew its congressional map to transform what was one of the last remaining swing districts in the South to a safe GOP seat. Lawmakers split the rectangular district into an hourglass shape that carved out Democratic voters in Raleigh and replaced them with a swath of rural counties reaching to the Virginia border. Swing seats, meaning a district a presidential candidate won by 5 percentage points or fewer in the previous election, are disappearing from the national map. For decades after World War II, the number of competitive seats in the House slowly eroded as the nation grew more polarized , voters were less likely to split their ticket and people moved closer to like-minded neighbors, creating Democratic strongholds in urban areas and Republicans ones across rural America. That decline accelerated the past year since President Donald Trump sparked a partisan redistricting battle. The number of swing districts fell from 45 to 37. There were 96 House seats that fit the modern definition of a swing seat in 1964, according to one count from the 1970s, when the shrinking number of such districts was first noted. That means the overwhelming majority of House seats are effectively won in primaries , with the support of only a fraction of highly ideological voters. Nickel saw the impact during his term. “The biggest divide I found in Congress wasn’t Democrat versus Republican, it was safe seats versus competitive seats,” Nickel said. “When your focus is on running a campaign where you talk to every single voter, you look at things differently and your focus is on solving problems.” Unite America, an organization pushing alternatives to party primaries, calculated that 87% of representatives elected to the House in 2024 were chosen by 7% of the country’s voters. “Voters don’t have any way of holding Congress responsible, except for a narrow window of swing districts,” Nick Troiano, the group’s executive director, said in an interview. “The least competitive election of our lifetimes will lead to the least accountable and least representative Congress of our lifetimes.” A narrow battlefield expands slightly in unpredictable midterm year Republicans are hoping the narrow range of competitive seats limits what Democrats can win on Nov. 3. “Both sides are fighting over a narrow House battlefield,” said Mike Marinella, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Campaign. “It’s a knife fight in a dark alley.” The alley may be widening this year , but it still is an alley. Democrats have expanded their political targets, with the unpopular Iran war and voters angry about high prices. There is a long-standing debate among academics as to how much of the decline can be blamed on partisan-motivated redistricting , known as gerrymandering, and how much on Americans’ increasing proclivity to live among like-minded people who vote the same way. Multiple studies have found that , without partisan gerrymandering, the House would have about double the number of competitive seats it has now. Studying the math and making a decision Nickel decided not to run for reelection after studying election returns dating to 2016 and finding that no Democratic incumbent had held on in a seat where Trump took 55% or more of the vote. Trump received 58% of the vote in the new district. Nickel eventually ran for district attorney of Wake County, the deeply Democratic county that was largely cut out of the 13th District. He won his primary and will take office in January. No Republican ran. That highlights how North Carolina, and the country, have effectively become segregated by political party. Only 15% of North Carolina’s voting precincts could be classified as politically competitive, according to Michael Bitzer, a political scientist at Catawba College. “For the average North Carolinian, depending on where they live, if they drive an hour in any direction they will be in a very different North Carolina,” he said. That certainly is the case traversing from the old 13th District to the new one, anchored in subdivisions and soybean and tobacco farms that stretch away from Raleigh. Here, few are talking about the congressional race. They see no reason to vote for anyone other than a Republican. “It’s just what I’ve always been,” said Linda Long, 62, a Republican in the town of Roxboro who works at the local Walmart. Democrats make a play in a long-shot district This is what Paul Barringer is up against. The Democratic nominee against Knott hopes for an upset in a year when even GOP members in safe seats like the 13th District are running scared. Neither Knott’s office nor his campaign responded to a request for an interview. Barringer, a former healthcare lawyer who returned to the tree farm in the district where he grew up, said he was previously a Republican but switched parties to run, hoping he could attract voters of all stripes. “I think people are disgruntled about things that are happening,” Barringer said. “They want people who will find ways to work together.” National Democrats added the seat to a list that could flip in such a favorable environment. But many doubt it. “They’re blowing smoke,” Linwood Parker, the 78-year-old mayor of Four Oaks, said of Democrats’ hopes they could win the district. Parker is a lifelong Republican who knows that gerrymandering is a decades-old tradition in North Carolina. Democrats used to do it until they lost power in the 2010 wave. Now Republicans do it. “Redistricting is just one of the levers that when Republicans, when they are in control, have to touch,” Parker said. “Otherwise it’s like saying, when we play this baseball game, we’re going to have three outs, we’ll give you two.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/us-house-district-once-political-143313840.html

item.title: Trump says noncitizen voting is a threat. A New York woman's arrest complicates the picture.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
An upstate New York woman who says she only recently learned she wasn’t born in the U.S. has been charged with voting illegally, one of the latest arrests touted by the Trump administration as it hunts for noncitizen voters ahead of the midterm elections. Marva Cook was adopted as a toddler and had always assumed she was a U.S. citizen, she told Homeland Security investigators earlier this month, according to the criminal complaint. But in searching for her biological mother, the 66-year-old Syracuse resident, who starred on Syracuse University’s women’s basketball team decades ago, said she discovered she had a German birth certificate. Federal prosecutors say Cook has had a green card for several years now, but she still cast ballots in recent elections despite not having citizenship. She faces a single federal charge of voting by an alien stemming from her vote in the 2022 midterms. The misdemeanor offense carries a maximum sentence of one year in prison and a fine up to $100,000, if convicted. Cook can also face deportation, under federal law . Cook says she has faith in God and support from community Reached by phone Friday, Cook declined to discuss the criminal case, her voting record or her past efforts at becoming a citizen. But she said she was “not thrilled” by her court appearance Wednesday as she was placed in shackles despite having voluntarily turned herself in just hours earlier. “It was a difficult time,” Cook said. “I’m about kindness and service and doing for others as I want to be treated.” She also said she appreciated the outpouring of support of community members, a number of whom accompanied her to court Wednesday. “The prayers and the support is a big part of how I will get through this,” Cook said. “I have a deep faith that God will get me through it.” Cook’s lawyer, Paul Tuck, also declined to discuss details of the criminal case Friday other than to say there are no upcoming hearings or filing deadlines. There are no pending immigration proceedings, he added, but Cook has an immigration lawyer in the event that changes. Spokespersons for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement didn’t immediately respond to emails seeking comment. Cook is latest arrest in Trump’s nationwide crackdown on noncitizen voting First Assistant U.S. Attorney John A. Sarcone III, whose upstate New York office is prosecuting the case, said Cook's arrest showed “voter fraud is rampant” in the state. Other federal agencies amplified the statement on social media, even as the administration’s own investigations have demonstrated that such instances are incredibly rare and been shown not to change the outcome of elections. “We cannot and will not allow the votes of American citizens to be canceled out by noncitizens illegally voting in our elections,” the Homeland Security wrote in a post on X that included Sarcone's statement. In California, federal authorities on Monday charged more than two dozen legal permanent residents with illegally casting ballots or registering to vote. Weeks earlier, 10 people were charged in Minnesota with illegally voting over the last three elections. Supporters say Cook is a valuable member of the community Cook’s supporters, meanwhile, described her as a vital part of the local community where she had lived nearly all of her life and had starred in college basketball. The Syracuse University athletics department confirmed Cook was the team’s leading scorer in the 1979-80 season, averaging 15 points per game. She also holds the school record for most steals in a single season. Fred Daley, pastor at All Saints Church, said Cook is an active member of the parish who for years has been the church’s go-to Easter Bunny, decked out in full costume during the spring holiday season. “If the government wanted to make a case, they chose the wrong person,” he said. “She’s a poster child of an amazing person. She’s highly respected throughout the community.” Dale Avers, a parishioner who has known Cook for almost 20 years, described her as a “person of service” who “never sought limelight.” She said Cook supports low-income families and youth as the YMCA’s community school program director. “I’m in total shock that they’re putting this much effort into this,” Avers said. “They understood the story. There was no intent. There’s no malice. There was no deception involved.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/york-state-woman-charged-voting-210057822.html

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, said she is "deeply distressed" by the news that her father, Thomas Markle, is under investigation over claims he possessed images containing child sexual abuse in his home. "I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. "I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families. President Donald Trump dismissed polls showing his approval rating falling ahead of November’s midterm elections , insisting Americans should trust his claim that his support is closer to 60 percent. In an interview with The Washington Examiner ’s Byron York, published Saturday, Trump called the polling figures “fake” when asked about a RealClearPolitics average showing 38.8 percent of Americans approved of his job performance, while 60.4 percent disapproved. “It’s fake,” Trump said. When York pressed him on what he believed his actual approval rating was, Trump rejected the figures and insisted his support was much higher. “The job approval, they said it’s 37, 38?” Trump asked. “I’m not at 38.” President Donald Trump dismissed polls showing his approval rating slipping ahead of November’s midterms as ‘fake,’ claiming his support is closer to 60 percent (AFP/Getty) Trump continued: “I don’t believe I could be beaten by anybody. I think that if I needed it, which I don’t, I think 60.” Trump pointed to his strong support among Republican voters and his MAGA base as evidence of his higher approval rating. However, national polling has consistently shown a less favorable picture of the president’s standing. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted between October 16 and 19 found that 34 percent approved of his performance and 65 percent disapproved. A Pew Research Center survey conducted September 28 through October 4 found that just 30 percent of Americans approved of Trump’s performance, while 68 percent disapproved. A separate New York Times /Siena College poll released this week put his approval rating at 34 percent, which the newspaper said was the lowest for a president approaching midterm elections since Harry Truman’s 33 percent in 1946. Trump’s rejection of polling figures comes amid a controversy involving The New York Times and Wedgewood Research, a polling firm that acknowledged producing fabricated polling numbers as part of a social experiment. The newspaper said it did not use the disputed polls when calculating Trump’s job approval rating. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found that just 34 percent approved of Trump’s job performance (Reuters) To support his claim that he remains popular, Trump pointed to an analysis by CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten showing the president’s support among MAGA Republicans remains near 100 percent. Enten reported that Trump received 99 percent of the MAGA Republican vote in the 2024 election and had a 98 percent approval rating among MAGA Republicans in September. “I think I’d be in the 60s now. Now, in the Republican Party, I’m way up. Show him the 99 percent. Have you seen it?” Trump said. However, Enten also found that Trump’s net approval rating on inflation fell from +8 points in 2024 to -45 ahead of the midterms . This week, Enten called the president’s polling situation “a five-alarm Trumpster fire” after a Reuters/Ipsos survey put Trump’s approval rating at 31 percent, the lowest recorded for him across both of his presidential terms. Despite the unfavorable figures, Trump continued praising Enten and CNN for polling that reflects his support among Republican voters. “They did do some nice polls on me, I must say. If CNN keeps doing those polls, I’ll like them more and more,” Trump said. item.title: Stocks make up more of Americans' assets than ever
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Your parents' nest egg was mostly bonds and savings accounts. Yours is mostly stocks. Stocks made up 48.2% of Americans' financial assets in the second quarter, counting everything from brokerage accounts to 401(k)s, according to the Federal Reserve's latest Financial Accounts data. That's the highest share in records going back to 1945. It tops the 38.7% reached at the height of the dot-com mania and the 41% hit after the 2021 meme-stock frenzy. Federal Reserve, Yahoo Finance The cash pile looks small by comparison. Households hold about $74 trillion in stocks against roughly $20 trillion in bank deposits and money market funds — a record $3.65 in stocks for every dollar of cash. So much for all that money waiting on the sidelines. Federal Reserve, Yahoo Finance Who 'Americans' really are There's some fine print. The Fed's household category is a catch-all that also includes nonprofits, and the central bank says its estimates for the group are "largely residual, derived from other sectors' data." The ownership is lopsided, too. The richest 1% of households own about half of all stocks and stock funds, and the top 10% own 88%, according to the Fed's distributional data . The bottom half owns about 2%. America isn't all in on stocks. Wealthy America is. Most of the climb also came from rising prices, not a buying spree. When stocks rally and everything else sits still, stocks take up a bigger slice of the pie on their own. What it has meant for returns History suggests a crowded trade tends to deliver less. When stocks made up less than 20% of household financial assets, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) went on to gain a median of about 11% a year over the next decade, according to Yahoo Finance calculations using price returns since 1951. When the share topped 30%, that fell to about 5%. The logic is simple. A low share means plenty of money is left to move into stocks, usually at bargain prices. A high share means much of that buying has already happened, and valuations are stretched. Federal Reserve, Yahoo Finance It's a decade-long signal, not a timing tool. Most of the high readings came from the late-1990s bubble and the years before the 2008 financial crisis. Today's level is beyond anything in the record. What it can do is prompt a portfolio checkup. An investor who set a 60/40 mix of stocks and bonds at the start of 2023 and never rebalanced would now have about 73% in stocks, by Yahoo Finance calculations. That's a lot more risk than they signed up for. A cushion, for now With this much wealth tied to the market, a sell-off like the one hitting AI stocks can dent consumer spending faster than it used to. Household balance sheets still have room to absorb one. Household assets have climbed to more than 10 times liabilities on "surging equity wealth," BofA Global Research economist Aditya Bhave wrote in a Sept. 24 report. Even if stocks fell 20%, the ratio "would only drop to 9.5," still higher than at any point before the second half of 2025, he wrote. The Fed's next update arrives Dec. 10, and a rough Yahoo Finance estimate puts the stock share near 49%, another record. You don't have to wait that long. The allocation that counts is the one on your own brokerage statement. Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication. Jared Blikre is the global markets and data editor for Yahoo Finance. Follow him on X at @SPYJared or email him at jaredblikre@yahooinc.com . item.title: Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat engulfed in flames as police detain suspect
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
More than 200 firefighters are at the scene in Bavaria - Getty Images Police have detained a suspect after a fire destroyed Adolf Hitler ’s German mountain retreat. Around 200 firefighters were deployed to the Eagle’s Nest, a remote residence at the top of Obersalzberg mountain in the Bavarian Alps, but narrow access roads and the building’s isolated location hampered their efforts. Firefighters found the Kehlsteinhaus residence “completely ablaze” when they arrived, police said. Emergency services were alerted at 9.52pm local time (8.52pm BST) after a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm. By Saturday, the building had been destroyed, and authorities said it was unclear whether any parts could be salvaged. German media reported that the fire had been burning for more than 12 hours and that nobody had been inside. Flames engulfed the Kehlsteinhaus, known as the Eagle’s Nest, on Friday night - Getty/Ferdinand Dorfler-Farthofer The man who was arrested, 33, suffers from mental health issues, the German public prosecution service said. He has been admitted to a psychiatric institution. He was stopped by police because the motorcycle he was riding had no number plate, and was found to have injuries to one of his hands that may have been caused by the fire. If convicted he could face up to a decade in prison for arson, but his mental health could be a mitigating factor. Lisa Maier, a police spokesman, said the building was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”. Firefighters were also hampered by the narrow road linking the retreat to Obersalzberg, which is usually closed to cars. Bad weather and water shortage also made extinguishing the fire difficult. Firefighters had to stop battling the blaze for several hours for safety reasons. Hitler’s former retreat is at an altitude of 6,000ft in Obersalzberg - AFP/Getty Images Joachim Herrmann, the Bavarian interior minister, said the Eagle’s Nest, which is owned by the German state, would be rebuilt. “Surely we can’t leave a ruin standing?” he said when asked about the building, adding there were no concrete plans yet “only 12 hours after the fire”. He admitted that “difficult” conversations would have to be held, but added it had been a popular tourist destination for years and was also a place of remembrance. The building was insured and the rebuilding costs would not have to be covered by the taxpayer, he said. The Italian foreign minister, left, visited Hitler at the Eagle’s Nest in 1939 - Getty/Galerie Bilderwelt The Kehlsteinhaus, nicknamed the Eagle’s Nest, was built in 1938 to host dignitaries and stands close to the Berghof, Hitler’s former summer residence located further down the mountain. Workers were forced to labour through the night during the winter of 1938 to finish the building in time for Hitler’s birthday in April 1939. Its lavish interior included a red Italian marble fireplace presented by Benito Mussolini, the Italian dictator. Allied soldiers later chipped pieces off it as souvenirs. The residence’s altitude and remoteness made it difficult for firefighters to access it - KERSTIN JOENSSON / AFP via Getty Images Hitler visited the Eagle’s Nest at least 14 times, although it was used largely to entertain foreign guests and diplomats. After the Second World War, the building served as an Allied command post until 1960, when it was returned to the state of Bavaria and designated a historic monument. The nearby Berghof residence was heavily damaged in a British air raid on April 25, 1945, before retreating SS troops set it on fire days later. item.title: DOJ charges government contractor with leaking secrets to journalist girlfriend
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Daniel Trotta Oct 23 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department accused a government contractor on Friday of leaking national defense information to his girlfriend, the publisher of a Substack newsletter. The FBI arrested Ian Brinksman, ‌42, on Friday following a search of his Washington home, a Justice Department statement said. Prosecutors charged ‌him with unlawfully transmitting national defense information. A federal public defender representing Brinksman declined to comment. “As alleged, Brinksman reached far outside his own duties ​to obtain some of our Nation’s most closely held secrets and handed them to a romantic partner he knew intended to publish them,” John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security, said in the statement. “That is not carelessness. It is a betrayal of his oath and the American people who entrusted him to fulfill his duties honorably,” Eisenberg ‌said. Brinksman held a top secret security clearance ⁠while working as an employee of a US government agency and later as a developer for systems integration for a private contractor working for the same agency, prosecutors said. According ⁠to the sworn affidavit of an FBI agent investigating the case, Brinksman repeatedly accessed classified intelligence reports and then communicated with the journalist. The affidavit also cites phone records, database access logs, badge-swipe records, emails and other evidence. The affidavit only ​identifies ​the journalist as "Individual 1," but it cites excerpts from articles ​she published. "A fundraising article reportedly published by ‌Individual 1 in September 2026 stated 'over the past year (Individual 1 has) published reporting based on classified (relevant U.S. government agency) assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about,'" the affidavit reads. That quote appears in a September 28 piece published on the Capital & Empire online newsletter authored by Aída Chávez. "Over the past year, I’ve published reporting based on classified CIA assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about," wrote Chávez, whose profile on the site ‌notes that she worked for the Nation and other outlets ​before she launched the newsletter. Chávez did not respond to an email ​message seeking comment. Investigators allege that on at least ​five occasions in 2026, Individual 1 published Substack articles containing information that mirrored the classified reports, ‌some at the top secret level. On some ​of those dates, Chávez published ​articles that cite classified reports, some of them attributed to the CIA. According to a LinkedIn profile bearing Brinksman's name, he worked for Deloitte as a manager and as a senior strategy security consultant after having ​worked as a US State Department ‌foreign service officer on dates corresponding to those outlined in the Justice Department statement. The State Department ​declined to comment. Deloitte did not respond to requests for comment. (Reporting by Daniel Trotta in Carlsbad, ​California; Editing by Tom Hogue, Sergio Non, Rod Nickel) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/us-accuses-government-contractor-leaking-025315584.html

"There is a Fake News report out there that I am going to remove the White House Press Room and bring back the old Swimming Pool, which lies directly underneath. Although I may move the Fake News to a less obnoxious location, the old swimming pool will never be brought back. I NEVER even thought to do such a stupid thing!" Trump has regularly called out what he considers ​unfair reporting about his administration. In September, the president sought to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House , saying he was frustrated by their reporting "fake news." A federal judge ordered the White House on Oct. 13 to continue allowing access to reporters from those outlets, although the Trump administration is contesting the ruling. Prior to that, Trump banned the Associated Press in February 2025 when the outlet declined to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America in its coverage. A federal judge ordered the restrictions lifted in April 2025. What is the White House Briefing Room? Since 1970, the White House press corps has met in the press briefing room, which was constructed during President Richard Nixon's term. The small theater was designed especially for television news coverage. The room was renamed the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room on Feb. 11, 2000, in honor of James Brady, the White House press secretary who was shot and seriously injured in an assassination attempt on President Ronald Reagan on March 30, 1981. Reagan was also shot in the incident and spent a dozen days in the hospital recovering, according to the George W. Bush White House Archives . A 2006 renovation led to improved work spaces, along with better online connections, lighting, and cooling; President George W. Bush reopen the renovated briefing room on July 11, 2007. item.title: Six Flags signals Goliath roller coaster will reopen after fatal fall at Georgia park
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
In this aerial view, the train of the Goliath roller coaster is seen on the track where it was evacuated at Six Flags Over Georgia on October 14 in Austell, Georgia. - Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images Six Flags will add seat belts to Goliath and other roller coasters with similar restraints following the death of a man who fell from the ride at Six Flags Over Georgia earlier this month. The company’s CEO said in a statement Friday that Goliath remains closed pending safety reviews and clearances following the death of Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old Atlanta resident and “cherished member” of a public charter school, who fell from the coaster on October 12 . Several other parkgoers were injured, including four minors, police said. In a statement addressed to guests and passholders, Six Flags President and CEO John Reilly said the company is reinforcing safety precautions across its parks, including installing seat belts on the Goliath, and has engaged independent engineers and ride inspection specialists to review safety procedures across its attractions. Goliath, a 3.5-minute ride reaching 70 mph and a height of 200 feet, features a waist restraint but does not have an over-the-shoulder harness . The addition of seat belts marks a significant change to the ride’s restraint system as investigators continue to examine what happened. “Safety has always been fundamental to the experience we provide for our guests,” Reilly said, adding that the company is committed to evaluating the findings and taking appropriate action. “Safety also depends on the dedicated teams who operate and maintain our attractions every day. Our ride operators complete a comprehensive, multi-stage training program that includes classroom instruction, hands-on training and supervised, on-the-job experience, with additional instruction and evaluation provided as necessary,” he continued. The Goliath roller coaster train sits on the track where riders were evacuated at Six Flags Over Georgia. - Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images Goliath and eight other rides at five additional Six Flags parks remain temporarily closed out of an abundance of caution, according to the company. Six Flags said its parks remain open, with more than 220 roller coasters operating across its properties. Where the investigation stands Preliminary information gathered at the scene from witnesses and employees indicated Kariem had been ejected from the ride, the Cobb County Police Department’s Major Crimes Unit said. He struck other riders before falling beneath the roller coaster, where he was found “unresponsive and not breathing,” police said in a statement. One witness, CiCi Nelson , told CNN she was in line to ride Goliath when a cart pulled up with an empty seat and other riders in hysterics. She said the safety bar on the empty seat appeared loose, and another young passenger appeared to be covered in blood and injured. Emergency personnel quickly arrived, and she and others were asked to evacuate the area. The announcement of the new seat belt installations follows the reopening of Six Flags Over Georgia last Friday, when visitors returned for the park’s annual Halloween Fright Fest events. Goliath remained closed as families entered the park, and officials offered no new findings about the fatal incident. Georgia authorities are investigating the death, reviewing evidence, equipment and documentation to determine whether state safety requirements were followed, according to a statement last week from Georgia Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner John King. Cobb County police are assisting state and park officials. CNN has reached out to Cobb County, Cobb County Police and the Georgia Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner for an update on the investigation into Kariem’s death and comment on Six Flags’ plans to add seat belts to Goliath and other coasters. As the investigation remains underway, CNN analysis has revealed alleged maintenance issues and guest injuries at several Six Flags parks. CNN’s review of safety records from 2016 through 2026 found that Goliath appeared to have passed annual state safety inspections. The coaster’s most recent inspection, on March 16, reported no violations, deficiencies, citations or red tags, according to King. A separate inspection report earlier this year noted that bushings, which are components that help reduce vibration, on the coaster needed replacement, according to CNN affiliate WSB. “I know trust is earned through actions and not words,” Reilly said. “As CEO of Six Flags, I take that responsibility personally.” CNN’s Isa Mudannayake, Karina Tsui, Isabel Rosales, and Julianna Bragg contributed to this report.
